extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of combustion turbine EGUs, power sector stakeholders, regulated entities, environmental lawyers, and policy commenters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria the EPA used to evaluate and select the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and related compliance options for new and reconstructed base load and intermediate load combustion turbine electric generating units (EGUs) in the NSPS rulemaking. Includes technical, timeline, cost, availability, and legal/administrative considerations for CCS and hydrogen co-firing pathways.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead time / timeline for CCS deployment
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPA must allow sufficient lead time for industry to design, plan, permit, engineer, and construct carbon capture, transport, and storage (CCS) systems; baseline S&L capture plant schedule ~6.25 years while an extended S&L schedule for new combustion turbines is ~7 years. EPA set compliance dates (e.g., January 1, 2032) reflecting these timelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA accounted for state plan processes (not applicable to new turbines) and practical project steps (FEED, right-of-way, permitting). The Agency may extend compliance dates where justified by competing demands on design/construct capacity, but here final dates reflect perceived sufficiency of a 7-year schedule (and, for some sources, a later compliance date of January 1, 2032).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated standard under CAA section 111
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as BSER, a control technology must be adequately demonstrated for affected sources and the EPA must show the industry can deploy the technology at scale within the compliance timeframe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate demonstration does not require widespread commercial use; EPA may set technology-forcing standards if reasonable and achievable. The Agency must balance encouraging technology adoption with ensuring standards are practicable given lead time and deployment capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: CCS as BSER for long-term coal-fired steam EGUs and base load turbines (90% capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA determined CCS at 90 percent capture as a standard of performance (component of BSER) for existing long-term coal-fired steam generating EGUs and used analogous timelines/components for base load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA views CCS as able to remove very high absolute amounts of emissions and as adequately demonstrated for affected sources; timelines and infrastructure demands factored into compliance date selection. EPA contrasted full (90%) capture with partial-capture approaches when assessing BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of industry deployment capacity and overlapping infrastructure demands
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must consider capacity constraints on designing, constructing, and operating CCS and associated pipeline/infrastructure which could overlap with demands from other sectors and sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such constraints can justify adjusted compliance schedules; EPA analyzed whether demands from coal, gas, and other projects necessitated longer delays for certain subcategories and set compliance dates accordingly (declining need to extend phase 2 date for base load turbines beyond coal EGU schedule).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed hydrogen co-firing BSER pathways (30% and 96% by volume) and election options
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed (but did not finalize) options including co-firing 30% (by volume) low-GHG hydrogen by 2032 (intermediate load) and for base load either CCS or (i) 30% low-GHG hydrogen by 2032 and (ii) 96% low-GHG hydrogen by 2038 as additional BSER components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA solicited comment on treating CCS and hydrogen co-firing as separate subcategories or as an either/or pathway. The Agency ultimately did not finalize the hydrogen co-firing pathway given uncertainties (notably cost and availability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for qualifying low-GHG hydrogen co-firing as BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed that (1) combustion turbines' capability to co-fire hydrogen be adequately demonstrated and (2) there be a reasonable expectation that necessary quantities of low-GHG hydrogen would be nationally available by the relevant compliance dates (2032 and 2038) at reasonable cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both technical capability and supply/cost expectations are required; if either is uncertain (especially nationwide availability and reasonable cost), EPA may not finalize hydrogen co-firing as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic/cost reasonableness for fuels and controls (hydrogen cost considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates projected delivered costs of low-GHG hydrogen (EPA used assumptions like $1/kg in baseline, revised to $1.15/kg in final modeling) and considers higher cost estimates a key factor against finalizing hydrogen co-firing as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA reviewed diverse analyst projections (DOE, McKinsey, BloombergNEF, Rhodium Group), Treasury rule uncertainties for tax credits, transport/storage costs, and capital equipment costs (e.g., electrolyzers). Higher-than-anticipated costs can preclude a technology from qualifying as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical feasibility of hydrogen co-firing (combustion turbine capability)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA notes multiple combustion turbine models from major manufacturers have successfully demonstrated the ability to combust hydrogen, and manufacturers expect future models capable of firing 100% hydrogen while limiting other pollutant emissions (e.g., NOx).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical demonstrations support feasibility, but feasibility alone is insufficient for BSER if supply/cost/availability criteria are unmet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty about nationwide availability of low-GHG hydrogen
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA requires sufficient certainty that significant quantities of low-GHG hydrogen will be available nationally by compliance dates at reasonable costs for it to be a BSER; current uncertainties prevented such a determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with models suggesting likely availability, EPA needs the full set of information (supply chain, costs, distribution) to support a nationwide reliance conclusion; EPA will monitor industry development and may reevaluate in future rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of life-cycle/production-method GHGs for hydrogen
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA emphasizes that production method matters: hydrogen combustion is zero-GHG at the stack, but hydrogen production can entail a range of GHG emissions; to ensure overall GHG benefits, the method of hydrogen production must be considered (well-to-gate emissions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposed but did not finalize limiting co-fired hydrogen to 'low-GHG' hydrogen; nevertheless, it states sources choosing to co-fire should prioritize low-GHG hydrogen to achieve net GHG reductions. Tracking and reporting complexities were identified as issues to address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market and policy developments as factors in EPA's decision (IRA/IIJA incentives)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considered federal incentives and programs (e.g., IIJA H2Hubs, IRA tax credits, LEEP funding under CAA section 135) that support low-GHG hydrogen supply chain development when assessing whether to require or define low-GHG hydrogen now.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence of large, fast-moving public/private programs counseled EPA against prescribing its own definitions and requirements immediately; these developments support EPA's expectation of increasing low-GHG hydrogen availability over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to require hydrogen used for compliance to be low-GHG (policy choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA chose not to finalize a requirement that hydrogen used for compliance be low-GHG hydrogen, citing ongoing Treasury rulemaking, emerging verification/reporting regimes, and other public/private developments that will define low-GHG hydrogen outside this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA nonetheless 'stresses' the importance of co-firing only low-GHG hydrogen to ensure overall GHG benefits and expects, based on market signals and incentives, that hydrogen used will generally be low-GHG even without a regulatory requirement now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-regulatory stakeholder engagement and potential future rulemaking on hydrogen production emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is opening a non-regulatory docket and engaging stakeholders on potential regulatory approaches for thermochemical hydrogen production emissions under CAA sections 111 and 112, and potential section 114 reporting requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural step signals EPA's intent to investigate regulating production-side emissions, which could influence future determinations about hydrogen as a BSER pathway and associated definitions/recordkeeping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed definition of low-GHG hydrogen (not finalized)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed defining low-GHG hydrogen as hydrogen produced with emissions of less than 0.45 kg CO2e/kg H2 (well-to-gate), aligning with the highest tier of IRC section 45V tax credits (eligible for $3/kg credit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA solicited comments on the proposal and alternatives but did not finalize a definition because it did not finalize hydrogen co-firing as BSER nor a low-GHG-only requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial capture CCS evaluation (rejection as BSER)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA rejected partial-capture CCS as BSER because partial capture yields lower emissions reductions and generally higher costs; 90% capture captures very high absolute emissions and benefits from economies of scale. Partial-capture designs may also forfeit tax-credit eligibility (e.g., IRC 45Q requiring design capture rates equivalent to 75% of baseline by mass).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated absolute emission reductions, cost-effectiveness, and tax-incentive interactions; lower capture rates may both reduce tax-credit returns and increase net cost, disfavoring partial capture as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combined Heat and Power (CHP) suitability criteria (rejection as BSER)
rubrics_metrics.description: CHP can lower emission rates and be economical when a facility primarily generates useful thermal output and is physically close to a thermal host with consistent, large thermal demand. However, practical limits (availability of adequately large thermal hosts, proximity, reliability of the host over the EGU life, financing risk) limit CHP applicability for new large EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA noted CHP usually supports smaller EGUs (several hundred MW max) and that dependency on a thermal host and potential host shutdown risk can hinder funding and sustained compliance, leading EPA to not select CHP as BSER for the targeted EGU categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid power plant considerations (solar thermal + fossil integration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hybrid plants integrating solar thermal with fossil-fired EGUs can improve overall conversion efficiency and lower incremental capital and O&M costs by leveraging existing fossil plant equipment; however, incremental costs (mirrors, piping, larger steam turbine) remain and feasibility/scale limitations apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered operational and cost tradeoffs (efficiency gains vs. incremental equipment costs) when evaluating hybrid plants as potential BSER candidates but did not determine them to be the BSER for the combustion turbine contexts in this rulemaking.
